stories.notes: No Supabase client credentials (project URL + anon key) existed locally at the start of this story -- only DATABASE_URL, a direct Postgres connection string used by the Python pipeline. Considered querying Postgres directly from Next.js with that string instead of requesting a new credential, but rejected it: Vercel serverless functions are ephemeral and would exhaust Supabase's direct-connection limit under real traffic, which is exactly why Supabase fronts Postgres with a pooler and recommends the REST API / supabase-js for serverless clients. Got the anon/publishable key from the user instead (frontend/.env.local, gitignored) and built on supabase-js, which also matches this story's own task_guidance ('Next.js frontend ... with data from Supabase'). Search is case-insensitive partial-name match (ilike), not exact match, since public users won't know a hospital's exact CMS-registered name string -- a stricter reading of 'a hospital name' was considered and rejected as needlessly hostile to the actual user. Verified against live production data, not just mocks: a hospital with all three fiscal years (ST ANTHONY SHAWNEE HOSPITAL, CCN 370149) renders 2023/2024/2025 in order, and a hospital with a genuine gap (ANSON GENERAL HOSPITAL, CCN 670781, missing FY2023) renders only its real 2 years plus an explicit 'reporting gap, not an error' note rather than a fabricated third row. The 'notes public data lag' criterion is a static, honest disclosure about CMS's filing-and-processing delay, not a computed lag figure -- there is no per-row lag data in the source to compute one from, and inventing a number would violate the project's own grounding guardrail (REQ-004).

tests_added: pipeline/test_early_warning.py (10 tests: each of the 3 criteria genuinely triggering, a fully healthy hospital with real falling-AR data correctly not flagged, missing metrics marked not_assessable rather than silently cleared, a real trigger winning over an unrelated missing metric, fewer-than-3-years and a real non-consecutive reporting gap both correctly not_assessable for the AR-trend criterion, and a falling AR trend correctly not_triggered rather than not_assessable)
stories.notes: Missing data is never treated as 'no problem': a criterion whose required metric is null is 'not_assessable', not 'not_triggered', and a hospital is only reported 'not_flagged' overall if every criterion was actually checked -- an early-warning system that quietly clears a hospital it couldn't check would defeat its own purpose. Precedence is flagged > not_assessable > not_flagged, so a real trigger is never hidden behind an unrelated missing metric (verified live: CCN 123456-style case with a real trigger + a missing metric elsewhere still flags). 'Days in A/R rising two years in a row' requires three CONSECUTIVE fiscal years, not just the latest three rows on file -- a hospital with a real reporting gap (missing fiscal year, an already-known pattern in this dataset) is correctly not_assessable for this one criterion rather than comparing non-adjacent years as if they were adjacent, which would silently understate what 'two years in a row' actually means. Flags are stored as one current-state row per hospital (early_warning_flags, PK provider_ccn), replaced on each run via ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, not appended as history -- re-running the evaluator is idempotent (verified live: ran twice against production, 274 rows before and after, no duplicates, identical distribution). Ran for real against all 274 hospitals in production Supabase: 257 flagged, 16 not assessable, 1 genuinely healthy (RICE MEDICAL CENTER, CCN 451312 -- 5.84% margin, 55.8 days cash, falling A/R). The high flag rate is a real finding about this population (rural/Critical Access hospitals nationally run on thin or negative margins), not a logic bug -- spot-checked individual hospitals' exact stored values against the flag verdict to confirm. Public read RLS on the new table, same as hospitals/cost_report_years: no management-company scoping exists yet since STORY-006 (row-level security) and STORY-005 (operator uploads, the thing that would actually need company-level scoping) aren't built. Reused the exact 'latest 3 fiscal years, ascending' query shape from frontend/src/lib/hospitalDetail.ts so the flag evaluator and the public Health Snapshot page can never disagree about which years count as 'the latest three'.

stories.notes: The story's own suggested approach (Next.js + Supabase storage, writing via supabase-js) could not actually work as suggested: the frontend only has NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY, and export_conversions/hospital_monthly_metrics (STORY-011) have RLS enabled with zero policies on purpose, so the anon key cannot read or write them. Raised with the user, who deferred to best judgment; built instead as a subprocess bridge: the Next.js API route (frontend/src/app/api/upload/route.ts) saves the uploaded file to a temp path and invokes the already-built, already-tested pipeline/export_normalizer.py (STORY-011) via child_process, rather than reimplementing hash-dedup, format detection, or the PHI gate in TypeScript. DATABASE_URL is read only by the Python subprocess from the repo-root .env -- never touches the Node process's environment or the browser bundle, so no new secret was needed. Extended export_normalizer.py for what STORY-005 genuinely needs that STORY-011 didn't: an is_duplicate flag on ConversionOutcome (STORY-011 only needed the end state to be correct on a re-run, never needed to report 'this was a repeat' as a distinct, user-facing outcome) and a --json CLI mode emitting one stable, parseable result line instead of human-readable text, so the Node bridge doesn't have to string-sniff output. Chose a JSON API response (with a real HTTP status per outcome: 200 ok, 409 duplicate, 422 needs_mapping/phi_rejected/failed, 400 malformed request, 500 unexpected) over a redirect-based no-JS form flow, since it's directly verifiable with curl and is the more idiomatic pattern for a file-upload interaction than the plain GET-search form STORY-003 used. Found two real bugs via live testing (Build-Break-Harden, not just the happy path): (1) the PHI gate's audit log line prints to stdout before the CLI's own --json result line, so a naive 'stdout is one JSON line' assumption would have broken the very first time a file was scanned -- fixed by having the parser take the last line, not assume a single line, and wrote a test locking this in; (2) request.formData() itself throws on an empty/malformed body, before any of the route's own file-presence validation runs, which surfaced live as an unhandled 500 with no body instead of a clean 400 -- fixed by wrapping the parse itself in a try/catch. Verified live end to end through the real running dev server (curl against the actual route, not a mocked handler): a fresh valid export returned 200 with 4 metrics normalized; the identical file re-uploaded returned 409 duplicate with zero new rows in export_conversions (confirmed by direct query, not just trusting the HTTP response); an unrecognized format returned 422 needs_mapping; a PHI-bearing export returned 422 with zero rows in either table; and the empty-body case returned a clean 400 after the fix. All live test rows and temp files cleaned up afterward. Did not build Supabase Storage for the raw file -- the acceptance criteria test accept/process/duplicate-rejection/hash-dedup, not file retrievability, and adding a storage bucket now would add integration surface (bucket policies, another credential) nothing here actually requires yet. Browser-based verification of the /upload page's client-side fetch flow was not possible in this environment (no browser automation tool available); verified the page renders correctly via direct HTTP fetch of its HTML and verified the exact API endpoint its fetch() call hits via curl instead -- a real but partial substitute for true in-browser testing, noted here rather than presented as full coverage. Follow-up: the user asked how to get real browser automation, since none was available in-session for the original verification. Installed @playwright/test and Chromium as a frontend dev dependency (matching this project's own stated standard for browser E2E work) rather than requiring a new MCP tool -- Playwright itself is the automation, run like any other test command. This resolves the 'no browser automation tool available' limitation noted above: the /upload page's actual client-side fetch flow is now driven by a real headless Chromium browser, not verified by curl-testing the endpoint separately. playwright.config.ts uses reuseExistingServer so it attaches to an already-running dev server instead of conflicting with one (found live: another dev server for this same repo was already running on port 3000 from an earlier session).

pipeline/test_row_level_security.py (6 tests against real Postgres RLS via session-level JWT claim simulation, not a mock: company A sees only its own hospital's monthly metrics, company B sees only its own, export_conversions and slipping_hospital_alerts are both also company-scoped, a user with no company membership sees nothing, and a fully anonymous session sees nothing. Opt-in only (RUN_RLS_INTEGRATION_TESTS=1) per this project's own rule that integration tests must never run automatically against production; skipped by default and confirmed skipped in the default `pytest pipeline/` run)
stories.notes: Sixth instance of the .colaberry/.hospulse numbering collision, but this time .hospulse's version ("Sign operators in and isolate each company's hospitals", REQ-008+REQ-019) was the more complete blueprint -- companies/company_members tables, Supabase Auth, RLS on every customer table, a test that signs in as two companies. Built .colaberry's literal 3 acceptance criteria using that blueprint's approach, but deliberately did not build a sign-in UI: .colaberry's criteria talk about 'accessing data', not a login form, and no story in the 13-story plan is explicitly 'build the sign-in screen' -- raised with the user and confirmed before building. Real gap found before writing any SQL: no auth system, no companies table, and no table anywhere recorded which hospitals a management company manages -- 'hospitals' itself is deliberately public data (STORY-003's free Health Snapshot), so a company doesn't own rows there, it manages a subset via a new company_hospitals join table. Verified live before writing policies, not assumed: auth.uid() reads request.jwt.claim.sub (confirmed via pg_get_functiondef); postgres (DATABASE_URL's role) has rolbypassrls=true, confirming the pipeline's existing writes were never subject to RLS and won't break; anon/authenticated already hold blanket ALL-privilege grants on every table (Supabase's schema-level default) -- RLS is the only real restriction, which is exactly why STORY-011/012's zero-policy tables were correctly fail-closed and not a mistake. RLS policies form a dependency chain (hospital_monthly_metrics -> company_hospitals -> company_members -> auth.uid()) and Postgres evaluates each referenced table's own RLS under the querying role's privileges, not the table owner's -- company_members needed its own 'see your own row' policy or the whole chain would silently resolve to zero rows for everyone, discovered by reasoning through the mechanism before writing SQL, not by a failing test after the fact. export_conversions had no hospital reference at all until this story -- added a nullable provider_ccn column (extending STORY-005/011's file again, same pattern as adding is_duplicate for STORY-005) populated from the first metric row's hospital when status=ok; needs_mapping and failed outcomes correctly leave it NULL rather than guessing, since needs_mapping genuinely never identifies a hospital. No changes needed to the upload route or export_normalizer.py's core normalization logic -- scoping happens entirely through company_hospitals joining on provider_ccn, not anything recorded at upload time. company_members.user_id is a bare uuid, not foreign-keyed to auth.users(id): no real sign-up/sign-in flow exists yet (out of this story's scope, confirmed with the user), so there are no real Supabase Auth users to reference. Verified live end to end through the real export_normalizer.py pipeline (not just direct SQL): a real upload correctly populated export_conversions.provider_ccn, and a needs_mapping upload correctly left it NULL. All live test rows (both the manual proof and the automated integration-test fixture, run twice to confirm re-runnability) cleaned up afterward, confirmed empty by direct query. Not yet committed to git as of this entry -- pending explicit go-ahead to commit.

stories.notes: Audited every REQ-015-named process (import, upload, normalization, email) before writing anything: all four were already idempotent by construction (ON CONFLICT upserts on natural keys in hcris_import.py/early_warning.py; a SHA-256 file-hash UNIQUE key in export_conversions for upload+normalization; a (company_id, week_of, recipient_email) UNIQUE key in weekly_briefing_emails for email) and three of the four already had a live double-run proof recorded in PROGRESS.md from their own stories. Two real, specific gaps survived that audit rather than everything being crediting-only: (1) no test anywhere exercised the interruption half of the acceptance criteria -- every existing proof was 'run twice from a clean start', never 'crash mid-run, then resume'. hcris_import.py's download_hcris_zip() already had the right shape (writes to a .part file, renames only on success) but it was undemonstrated; added 4 tests (offline, urlretrieve monkeypatched -- no real network) covering skip-if-already-downloaded, a stale .part left by a simulated crash not being mistaken for a completed download, and the existing retry/backoff path, which had zero test coverage before this story despite already being written. (2) export_conversions and weekly_briefing_emails already are execution-state logs in the sense the Trust criterion asks for (one row per unit of work, written on every outcome) -- hcris_import.py and early_warning.py had no equivalent, only their final upserted data tables, so a resumed run had nothing to point at as 'here is what the last run did'. Added a small shared pipeline/pipeline_run_log.py (start_pipeline_run/finish_pipeline_run) and wrapped both processes' run() in it -- not a new idempotency key (the natural-key upserts already made both safe to run twice before this table existed), purely the audit trail. Did not route export_normalizer.py or weekly_briefing_email.py through the same table: they already have a finer-grained log of their own (per-file, per-send) and duplicating that into a second table would be redundant, not stronger. Live-verified, not just unit-tested: applied the schema.sql migration to production Supabase, then ran early_warning.py twice back to back (274/274 hospitals, identical distribution both times, pipeline_runs shows 2 succeeded rows) and hcris_import.py --fiscal-year 2025 twice back to back (137/137 rows both times, pipeline_runs shows 2 succeeded rows, no growth in cost_report_years from the repeat run). Full pipeline/ suite: 124 passed, 1 skipped, zero regressions.

tests_added: pipeline/test_phi_guardrail.py (22 tests: header-based detection for all three REQ-009 categories -- patient names, birth dates, record numbers; an SSN-shaped-content fallback for a mislabeled column; false-positive avoidance on ordinary business dates; and the ingest gate proving rejection happens before storage and before the PHI value itself ever reaches the audit log)
stories.notes: REQ-009's own wording ('reject... before it is stored or logged') requires real gating behavior, not just a detector -- STORY-011's grounding_guardrail.py was built the same standalone way and stayed unticked until something actually calls it, so scan_file_for_phi() alone would not have earned these criteria. Added ingest_file_with_phi_gate(file_name, rows, store=, log_audit=): store is only called when the scan is clean, never for a rejected file (proven by test_gate_rejects_a_file_with_patient_names_before_storage / test_gate_rejects_a_file_with_birth_dates_before_storage asserting store was never called), and log_audit always receives a PhiAuditEntry naming the column and category that triggered rejection but never the row content itself (test_gate_audit_log_never_contains_the_raw_row_content, test_gate_birth_date_value_never_reaches_the_audit_log). store/log_audit are injected because the real Supabase write and logger do not exist yet (STORY-005, not started) -- STORY-005 plugs in the real implementations without changing this function. Two-layer detection: column-header match for all three categories (deterministic, matches how a real hospital-system export would label these fields) plus an SSN-content fallback for a column mislabeled with an innocuous header. Deliberately not attempted: generic content-based matching for names or dates by shape alone -- financial exports carry legitimate business dates (report date, posting date) and free text cannot reliably be classified as 'a name' without a model, so that would trade false rejections of clean ledger data for coverage the header check already provides in the realistic case; documented as a known limitation in the module docstring, not left silent.

tests_added: pipeline/test_export_normalizer.py (14 tests: two different vendor formats reconciling to the same standard metric names/values, unknown format correctly marked needs_mapping (including a fingerprint missing just one column), totals rows dropped without corrupting source_row provenance for the rows that follow, a malformed month producing a failed outcome rather than a crash, a missing per-row column producing failed rather than a crash, denial rate left None rather than a fake 0% when there are zero total claims, file-hash determinism for the idempotency key, CSV round-tripping, and the PHI audit log line being valid JSON that never carries the flagged cell value)
stories.notes: Built under .colaberry's STORY-011 definition (Convert Hospital System Exports to Standard Metrics, REQ-011, release r1) after finding this is a third instance of the .colaberry/.hospulse numbering collision already documented for STORY-010 and STORY-003: .hospulse's own STORY-011 is an unrelated cost-report-co-pilot story (REQ-015, release r4), and its own REQ-011 equivalent is fulfilled by .hospulse's STORY-008 instead, which is also not started. Followed the same precedent as before -- build .colaberry's definition, leave docs/stories/STORY-011.md un-rewritten since it reflects .hospulse's numbering repo-wide, not just this one file. No operator-upload path exists yet (STORY-005, not started), so 'an export from a hospital system' is raw file bytes handed directly to export_normalizer.run() -- the upload UI is out of this story's scope. Two illustrative vendor mappings (Epic, Cerner) prove the mechanism: mappings.detect_format() matches by exact column-fingerprint subset, never fuzzy/partial (confirmed live: an export missing even one expected Epic column falls through to needs_mapping rather than being forced through), and both vendors' distinct column layouts reconcile onto the same four standard metric names with identical values for the same underlying data (confirmed live). Column layouts for both vendors are illustrative -- no real Epic/Cerner export sample was available to build against, unlike hcris_import.py's worksheet citations which were all confirmed against a real downloaded file; a real vendor's mapping module would need a real sample to write against. Idempotency: export_conversions keyed on a SHA-256 of the raw file bytes (not the filename -- a re-uploaded file with a new name is still the same file, a corrected file with the same name is not), confirmed live that reprocessing identical content under a different filename returns the first run's outcome without a second audit row; hospital_monthly_metrics upserts on (provider_ccn, month, metric_name). Both new tables get RLS enabled with ZERO policies, deliberately -- this is a management company's private data, not public CMS data like hospitals/cost_report_years, and no per-company scoping exists yet (STORY-006, not started), so this fails closed rather than defaulting to the public-read policy the CMS tables use. Found mid-task that the whole-project PHI guardrail (REQ-009, STORY-010) applies to this ingestion path too and wasn't being called -- the same lesson this repo already learned once for STORY-011's own grounding_guardrail sitting unticked until something called it. Wired in phi_guardrail.ingest_file_with_phi_gate() rather than rebuilding detection: confirmed live that a hospital export carrying a 'Patient Name' column is rejected (PhiRejectedError, raised rather than folded into ConversionOutcome.status so a caller can't mistake a security rejection for a normal outcome) before either export_conversions or hospital_monthly_metrics is touched, with a structured stdout audit line containing the flagged column/category/reason but never the cell value itself; a clean file re-verified working end to end afterward. Extracted the previously-duplicated load_env() into pipeline/env.py once this third file needed it, per this project's own 'three is the threshold' composition rule -- hcris_import.py and early_warning.py now import it instead of each defining their own copy; full 76-test suite re-verified green after the refactor. stories.notes: REQ-016 ("surface a slipping hospital at least 4 weeks earlier than the operator's current reporting cycle") names no timestamped 'operator reporting cycle' anywhere in this system to literally measure elapsed time against. Confirmed with the user before building: the defensible reading is structural, not a literal duration -- detection runs automatically the moment a month's export is normalized (STORY-011), rather than waiting for an operator's own roughly-monthly manual review, which is what '4 weeks earlier' means in practice. Verified live: as soon as an August export was normalized, the hospital was flagged 'slipping' in the same run, with no separate review step in between. REQ-016 also gives no numeric thresholds, unlike REQ-004/REQ-005's explicit 'below 0%' / 'below 30 days' -- also confirmed with the user before building rather than inventing an unstated magic number: each of the 3 criteria (cash_on_hand declining, denial_rate_pct rising, ar_balance rising) triggers on a plain month-over-month directional change between the two latest consecutive months, mirroring STORY-004's own 'two in a row' shape for its annual AR-trend criterion but requiring only 2 months instead of 3 years since monthly data updates much faster. Same missing-data philosophy as STORY-004: a criterion with a null required metric, or whose two latest months are not genuinely consecutive calendar months (a gap, not just 'the two most recent rows'), is not_assessable, never a guessed verdict; precedence is slipping > not_assessable > not_slipping so a real trigger is never hidden behind an unrelated gap (verified: a missing cash_on_hand value alongside a genuine denial-rate spike still flags). slipping_hospital_alerts gets RLS enabled with ZERO policies, deliberately different from early_warning_flags' public-read policy -- this table is derived from hospital_monthly_metrics (STORY-011's private, operator-uploaded data), not public CMS data, and no per-company scoping exists yet (STORY-006, not started). One current-state row per hospital, replaced via ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE on each run, same as early_warning_flags -- confirmed live idempotent (re-running immediately after produced the same single row, not a duplicate). Verified live end to end through the real STORY-011 pipeline, not synthetic rows inserted directly: normalized two real consecutive months' exports for one hospital (cash dropping $200k to $150k, denial rate rising 5% to 9%, AR balance unchanged), then ran the detector and confirmed it correctly flagged 'slipping' with cash_on_hand_declining and denial_rate_rising both triggered (exact before/after values stored) and ar_balance_rising correctly not_triggered (unchanged is not a false positive). All live test rows deleted from the production tables afterward.
